what_happened: For about two days (2026-10-14 to 2026-10-15) the operator ran Athena's own steward and audience work queue by hand. They used shell scripts to push items through one at a time and approved implementation-rung items that were within limits. Athena had no built-in way to drain its queue or to approve in-limit items on its own. Those features arrived later as #94 (drain) and #97 (in-limit approval).
cause: Athena's queues were built to produce items before anything consumed them. Routine steps, such as draining and approving work already inside defined limits, were left as operator tasks and never became system behavior. Nothing flagged repeated manual operation as a gap to close. The scripts also ran outside the job lifecycle, so the need only showed up after the operator had done the work many times.
prevention: Ship every queue with its consumer. Any queue Athena writes to needs a built-in drain path and an automatic approval rule for items inside stated limits. Items outside the limits go to the operator. Operator-run scripts against Athena's own state should be logged as interventions, so repeated hand-driving is flagged as a missing capability. #94 (drain) and #97 (in-limit approval) cover the current queues. The design rule and the logging would cover future ones.
proposed_request: Make it a rule that any new Athena work queue ships with a drain command that processes its items without operator scripts, and with automatic approval of items inside the stated limits. Items outside the limits must still go to the operator. Add a check at queue creation that fails if a queue has no drain path. Also log any operator-run script that changes Athena's queue state as an intervention. Done when a test queue with in-limit and out-of-limit items drains with no manual steps, the out-of-limit items wait for the operator, and each manual queue action appears in the intervention log.
